passage:
Third week of the monsoon holidays in Bishnupur, and Anirban's tabla practice had gone grey. The first days had been thrilling: new bols, Baba recording him on the old phone, Thakuma clapping from the veranda. Now it was the same teen-taal, round and round, and his fingers still stumbled on the same fast phrase. Ustadji said it would take months.
From the lane came Jeevan's whistle. "Anirban! Fishing at the big pond, everyone's going!"
Anirban looked at the tabla, then at the rain-washed lane. One day off won't matter, he thought. I practised yesterday. I'll do double tomorrow.
He didn't feel like practising at all. Nothing of the early excitement was left to pull him to the mat. He sat there, half up and half down, listening to Jeevan's footsteps slow outside the gate.

qa.q: What did Anirban's fingers still stumble on?
qa.a: His fingers still stumbled on the same fast phrase.

qa.q: How does Anirban feel when Jeevan whistles, and what bargain does his mind make?
qa.a: He feels bored and torn, so he tells himself one day off won't matter because he practised yesterday and can do double tomorrow.

qa.q: What could help Anirban keep going now that the excitement has worn off?
qa.a: He could do a short, fixed practice before joining Jeevan, so the habit rests on a simple rule rather than on whether he feels like it.

qa.q: What might Jeevan think, waiting outside the gate?
qa.a: Jeevan probably just wants his friend at the pond and may not realise Anirban is torn between fun and a practice that has gone dull.

grounding: Shows a teenager in week three of tabla practice, bored by slow progress and bargaining that skipping one day won't hurt.

passage:
Day nineteen of the plan Lars had copied into his notebook: jog to the harbour and back, forty push-ups, every evening. In week one he'd felt like an athlete. Now, on Bergen's third straight day of rain, he checked his arms in the bathroom mirror and saw exactly the same arms.
His brother Daniel, home from university, glanced up from the sofa. "Going out in that?"
Lars pulled on one shoe and stopped. It's just rain, he told himself. Then another voice: skip today, the plan says rest days are fine anyway. It didn't, actually.
He sat on the bottom stair, one shoe on and the other in his hand, feeling nothing like the boy who had started this. Daniel said nothing, just raised an eyebrow.
Lars tied the second lace slowly, not because he wanted to, but because he'd said he would.

qa.a: Jog to the harbour and back, forty push-ups, every evening.

qa.q: What does Lars's thought 'the plan says rest days are fine anyway' reveal?
qa.a: He feels discouraged and bored, so his mind bargains for a skip, even inventing a rule, because his arms look exactly the same.

qa.q: Why did tying the second lace matter, and what might help on the next rainy day?
qa.a: Lars went because he'd said he would, not because he felt like it; a shorter indoor version for rainy days could make discipline easier when mood is low.

qa.q: How might Daniel see his brother on the bottom stair?
qa.a: Daniel may recognise the struggle and chooses a raised eyebrow over a lecture, leaving the decision to Lars.

grounding: Illustrates week three of a fitness routine when results are slow, the mind bargains for a skip, and going depends on discipline rather than mood.
